title: What moved your money this month
intro: 2026 has been driven by an energy shock and an AI chip boom. India benefits from neither: it imports oil and has little chip exposure. September was a broad risk-off month, and only 16% of Indian sectors went up.
scoreboard_note: in rupees, for an Indian investor

scoreboard.means: If you hold an index fund or most equity mutual funds, this is roughly what your year looks like.

scoreboard.plain: The same money, put in America instead
scoreboard.means: American shares did well, and a weaker rupee made them worth even more back home. This is the cost of having everything in one country.
Gold went nowhere globally. For an Indian it still held its value, because the rupee fell and gold is priced in dollars.

scoreboard.plain: What your rupee is worth abroad
scoreboard.means: Your money buys this much less outside India than in January. Imported goods, foreign travel and overseas education all cost more.

scoreboard.plain: What the government pays to borrow
scoreboard.means: This sets the floor under everything else: your FD rate, your home loan, what a safe investment should return.
India buys over 80% of its oil from abroad. When oil rises, transport, packaging and food all follow, and the rupee weakens paying for it.

scoreboard.plain: How many shares are actually up
scoreboard.means: Out of every 100 listed companies, this many are higher than in January. When this is low, most portfolios are doing worse than the headline index suggests.

scoreboard.plain: How broad the last day was
scoreboard.means: On the most recent trading day, this share of market sectors rose. A low number means the fall was everywhere, not in one corner.

scoreboard.plain: What you pay for ₹1 of profit
scoreboard.means: Buy the index today and you pay this many rupees for each rupee of annual profit those companies make. Higher means you are paying more for the same earnings.

tracker_groups.name: Economy and money
tracker_groups.blurb: Oil, rates and the rupee are where most shocks start. They explain what happened, and to what.

cards.why: India imports over 80% of its oil. Higher oil means higher inflation, a weaker rupee and pressure on margins.
Imports get costlier, but dollar assets gain in rupee terms. A slow grind, not a shock: volatility is about 5%.
cards.plain: What your rupee is worth abroad
cards.means: Imported things cost more. Money already invested abroad is worth more in rupees.

cards.why: The risk-free benchmark. Rising yields hurt long-duration debt funds and make stocks less attractive.
cards.plain: What the Indian government pays to borrow
cards.means: The safest return available in India. When it rises, shares have to work harder to look worth the risk.

cards.why: High US rates pull money out of emerging markets, including India.
cards.plain: What the American government pays to borrow
cards.means: When America pays more for safe money, global investors move money out of India to get it.

cards.why: A strong dollar usually means a weaker rupee and foreign selling.
cards.plain: How strong the dollar is worldwide
cards.means: A strong dollar usually means a weaker rupee and foreign investors pulling money out of India.

cards.why: The base price of money. Moves FD rates, EMIs, bond prices and stock valuations.
cards.means: The price of money in India. It moves your EMI, your FD rate and, eventually, share prices.

cards.why: Drives RBI decisions. Core shows whether price rises are spreading or temporary.
cards.means: If this is higher than what your savings earn, your money is quietly shrinking even while the number in the account grows.

cards.why: Negative real rates push money into stocks, gold and property.

watching.v: Cheap oil is one of India's biggest tailwinds. When it falls, most of the chain runs in reverse.
Three losing years so far. Stability would ease imported inflation and foreign selling.

points.t: Your equity funds are probably down this year.
points.b: India's 50 biggest companies are about 15% lower than in January. Most diversified equity funds will look similar.

points.t: It started with oil, not with shares.
points.b: Oil nearly doubled. India imports most of its oil, so the rupee fell paying for it, prices rose, interest rates stayed high, and shares got cheaper as a result. One thing pulled the next.
This describes a year that has already happened. The part you control is not the oil price. It is whether you keep investing through a bad stretch, and that is the whole of section three.
